extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians and researchers interested in IUT, arithmetic geometry, and Mochizuki's work (readers of theHigherGeometer blog)
extracted.subtask_description: A short blog announcement pointing readers to slides by Taylor Dupuy that present explicit computations in IUT, stated to be conditional on Corollary 3.12 of Mochizuki's third IUT paper. Emphasizes readability, links to supporting material, and the conditional/controversial status of the underlying corollary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit computations
rubrics_metrics.description: Slides present 'Explicit Computations in IUT' — the work is explicitly computational in nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The announcement emphasizes that the slides are focused on explicit computations (the title: 'Explicit Computations in IUT') and that they are modeled on prior YouTube videos; include worked examples and concrete calculations rather than only high-level abstraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditional statement of results
rubrics_metrics.description: The computations and statements are 'explicitly stated by Dupuy as being conditional on Corollary 3.12 in Mochizuki’s third IUT paper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about dependencies: if results rely on Corollary 3.12 or other unestablished claims, state that dependency clearly so readers understand the conditional nature of the conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community acceptance of underlying proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledges that 'the written proof of [Corollary 3.12] is not accepted by almost the entire number theory community.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate work in light of broader community acceptance: note whether critical ingredients (proofs/corollaries) are widely accepted or remain controversial; this affects how confidently subsequent computations or consequences can be treated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rendering in ordinary mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement of Corollary 3.12 is 'rendered in ordinary mathematics, rather than in the language of Frobenioids and their ilk.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer formulations in conventional mathematical language when possible to improve accessibility and facilitate verification by a wider audience rather than relying solely on specialized frameworks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplifying and isolating sound parts
rubrics_metrics.description: The slides aim at 'simplifying what seems like the sound part of Mochizuki’s work ... to ordinary mathematics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When presenting work that builds on a larger, controversial framework, isolate and simplify portions that appear robust so others can check and use them independently of the full original apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding opaque metaphors and alien structures
rubrics_metrics.description: Notes a benefit: 'no dismantling alien ring structures or odd metaphors about how school students get confused by logarithms.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor clear, standard mathematical explanations over opaque metaphors or highly idiosyncratic constructions that hinder understanding and verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide links and references for technical details
rubrics_metrics.description: Slides are 'modelled on his series of YouTube videos ... (and there are links to them in the slides, for technical details).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include pointers to additional material (talk videos, detailed notes, source papers) so readers can follow up on technical justifications and background.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readability of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: The post and commenter praise the slides as 'readable slides' and emphasize making the material 'ordinary mathematics' to enhance readability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for presentations (slides, notes) that are accessible and readable to the intended mathematical audience; readability encourages scrutiny and uptake.
